articles.text: Part 4 in a series Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. The MOSAIC Project The MOSAIC Project is a youth leadership project that provides extensive training in diversity and conflict-resolution for young adults and teens through Youth Leadership Training weekend retreats, held every March and August. High school and college-aged volunteers serve as mentors for students in 4th and 5th grade who participate in MOSAIC’s outdoor retreats. Volunteers are required to attend their own weekend training retreat before leading the sessions. To apply, visit mosaicproject.org/programs/ youth-leadership-project, or contact Youth Leadership Director Khemnes Fisher by phone at 452-3377 or by email at khemnes@ mosiacproject.org. Prisoner’s Literature Project The Berkeley-based Prisoner’s Literature Project is an all-volunteer grassroots nonprofit that has provided free books to prisoners for over 30 years. The organization is always looking for volunteers to answer letters, send out books, learn more about the prison system, and assist with fundraising or publicity efforts. Adult volunteers are encouraged to help, and youth volunteers aged 10 through 15 are welcome with a parent or guardian overseeing their work. Visit prisonlit.org/volunteer for more information. Oakland Museum Volunteering at the Oakland Museum of California gives adults and teens the chance to get more involved with a local museum, and an opportunity to learn more about the state’s rich history. The museum is always recruiting volunteers to assist with school groups, events, office work, and more. Informational sessions are offered several times a year, where museum staff discuss the various types of opportunities available. Learn more about orientation dates and apply to volunteer by visiting shiftboard.com/museumca. HandsOn Bay Area HandsOn connects community members with high-quality volunteer projects through an extensive network of local nonprofits and schools in need. There are always opportunities for kids and adults to volunteer with HandsOn across a variety of industries and skillsets, with venues including food banks, community gardens, libraries, and clothing distribution centers. Visit handsonbayarea. org to find projects that are accessible to volunteers of any age. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? articles.text: Editor: I am happy that PREC has publicly expressed its support for low-income housing in Moraga Canyon. Piedmont’s professional city staff and involved citizens have been trying hard to comply with State law and need all the support they can get. But PREC’s proclamation in the Post leaves at least this reader wondering why the group has weighed in now on this long-settled issue. articles.text: Piedmont residents who have experienced private property damage from storms in December and January may be eligible for federal funding for storm-related costs not covered by insurance. During the week of January 30, Alameda County was added to the “major disaster” declaration for California’s severe storms and flooding. This declaration allows the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to provide direct support to individuals and businesses in Alameda County. FEMA grants are available for up to $37,900 for property damage to a primary residence, or for ancillary costs, such as staying in a hotel while emergency repairs are made to the home, or increased childcare and medical expenses. Loans for storm relief are also available to homeowners, renters, and businesses through the federal Small Business Administration. These loans can be paid off over 30 years with interest as low as 4 percent. Loan types include: • Homeowners: Up to $200,000 to repair or replace a primary residence • Renters or homeowners: Up to $40,000 to replace or repair personal property, like clothing, furniture, cars, or appliances • Businesses: Up to $2 million to meet financial obligations or operating expenses during the storms To qualify for funding, applicants must meet FEMA eligibility guidelines and file a claim with their insurance provider. Federal support is available only to assist with costs not already covered by insurance, or to those who do not have insurance. How to apply Applications are due by March 16 and can be done online at DisasterAssistance.gov, or by phone at 1-800-621-3362, or in person at the Alameda County Disaster Recovery Center, 7001 Oakport Street, Oakland. articles.text: Did you know that residential buildings account for roughly half of Piedmont’s in-territory greenhouse gas emissions? Nearly all of the emissions from this sector come from natural gas used for heating and cooling. In addition to contributing to the climate crisis, gas appliances can create unhealthy levels of indoor air pollution. Luckily, transitioning to an all-electric home is becoming a more cost-effective option. The electrification nonprofit Rewiring America found 85% of U.S. households could save money on energy bills if they used modern all-electric appliances. Additionally, there are many rebates and incentives available to Piedmont homeowners. If you’re thinking about replacing your gas appliances with highly efficient electric ones, here are ten resources to help you get started electrifying. Additional incentives and rebates may be found through SwitchIsOn.org. 1. City of Piedmont Piedmont’s electrification rebate program launched in 2023. The city is offering an $800 rebate for heat pump water heaters, a $1,500 rebate for central air source heat pumps, a $750 rebate for mini split heat pumps, and a $500 rebate for panel upgrades. To learn more, visit the Rebates and Incentives page on the city’s Planning and Building Department website at bit.ly/3YWZ6qj. 2. BayREN BayREN offers a suite of rebates, including $1,000 for a heat pump, up to $2,950 for building shell upgrades (including attic and wall insulation, air sealing, and duct repair or replacement), and up to $1,100 in bonus measures for combining building shell upgrades with a heat pump. 3. California Energy Smart Homes California Energy Smart Homes offers a $5,550 rebate for single-family homeowners who convert all their gas appliances to electric. They also provide $3,550 to multifamily property owners who convert all gas appliances to electric. 4. Multifamily Energy Savings Program The Multifamily Energy Savings Program, administered by PG&E, offers $350 per ton on mini split heat pumps and a rebate of $305 for a heat pump water heater for multifamily properties. 5. Inflation Reduction Act The first phase of incentives through the landmark Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) are now available. Homeowners can claim tax credits for a range of energy-related upgrades, including $1,000 for an electric vehicle charger and $2,000 for a heat pump. 6. TECH Clean California The TECH program launched last year and due to a higher-than-anticipated response in PG&E service territory, incentives were temporarily suspended. Additional rebates for heat pumps (space and water heating) will launch this spring; stay tuned for future updates. 7. Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP) The California Public Utility Commission’s Self-Generation Incentive Program offers rebates for installing battery storage systems. The SGIP is administered by PG&E and will be offering rebates for heat pump water heaters this summer. 8. PG&E PG&E offers a variety of rebates for qualifying products such as induction cooktops, electric dryers, and portable batteries. Check out PG&E Energy Action Guide at guide.pge.com to get started. 9. Golden State Rebates Program The Golden State Rebates Program offers a $500 rebate on heat pump water heaters as well as discounts on smart thermostats and room air conditioners. Visit goldenstaterebates.com to learn more. 10. East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) EBCE offers several programs to make your home more energy efficient, including home solar + battery storage systems at pre-negotiated pricing and rebates of up to $1,700 for portable battery power stations for Medical Baseline customers, all at ebce.org. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions on electrification.

In addition to contributing to the climate crisis, gas appliances can create unhealthy levels of indoor air pollution. Luckily, transitioning to an all-electric home is becoming a more cost-effective option. The electrification nonprofit Rewiring America found 85% of U.S. households could save money on energy bills if they used modern all-electric appliances. Additionally, there are many rebates and incentives available to Piedmont homeowners. If you’re thinking about replacing your gas appliances with highly efficient electric ones, here are ten resources to help you get started electrifying. Additional incentives and rebates may be found through SwitchIsOn.org. 1. City of Piedmont Piedmont’s electrification rebate program launched in 2023. The city is offering an $800 rebate for heat pump water heaters, a $1,500 rebate for central air source heat pumps, a $750 rebate for mini split heat pumps, and a $500 rebate for panel upgrades. To learn more, visit the Rebates and Incentives page on the city’s Planning and Building Department website at bit.ly/3YWZ6qj. 2. BayREN BayREN offers a suite of rebates, including $1,000 for a heat pump, up to $2,950 for building shell upgrades (including attic and wall insulation, air sealing, and duct repair or replacement), and up to $1,100 in bonus measures for combining building shell upgrades with a heat pump. 3. California Energy Smart Homes California Energy Smart Homes offers a $5,550 rebate for single-family homeowners who convert all their gas appliances to electric. They also provide $3,550 to multifamily property owners who convert all gas appliances to electric. 4. Multifamily Energy Savings Program The Multifamily Energy Savings Program, administered by PG&E, offers $350 per ton on mini split heat pumps and a rebate of $305 for a heat pump water heater for multifamily properties. 5. Inflation Reduction Act The first phase of incentives through the landmark Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) are now available. Homeowners can claim tax credits for a range of energy-related upgrades, including $1,000 for an electric vehicle charger and $2,000 for a heat pump. 6. TECH Clean California The TECH program launched last year and due to a higher-than-anticipated response in PG&E service territory, incentives were temporarily suspended. Additional rebates for heat pumps (space and water heating) will launch this spring; stay tuned for future updates. 7. Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP) The California Public Utility Commission’s Self-Generation Incentive Program offers rebates for installing battery storage systems. The SGIP is administered by PG&E and will be offering rebates for heat pump water heaters this summer. 8. PG&E PG&E offers a variety of rebates for qualifying products such as induction cooktops, electric dryers, and portable batteries. Check out PG&E Energy Action Guide at guide.pge.com to get started. 9. Golden State Rebates Program The Golden State Rebates Program offers a $500 rebate on heat pump water heaters as well as discounts on smart thermostats and room air conditioners. Visit goldenstaterebates.com to learn more. 10. East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) EBCE offers several programs to make your home more energy efficient, including home solar + battery storage systems at pre-negotiated pricing and rebates of up to $1,700 for portable battery power stations for Medical Baseline customers, all at ebce.org. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions on electrification. Federal aid available for private property storm damage Piedmont residents who have experienced private property damage from storms in December and January may be eligible for federal funding for storm-related costs not covered by insurance. During the week of January 30, Alameda County was added to the “major disaster” declaration for California’s severe storms and flooding. This declaration allows the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to provide direct support to individuals and businesses in Alameda County. FEMA grants are available for up to $37,900 for property damage to a primary residence, or for ancillary costs, such as staying in a hotel while emergency repairs are made to the home, or increased childcare and medical expenses. Loans for storm relief are also available to homeowners, renters, and businesses through the federal Small Business Administration. These loans can be paid off over 30 years with interest as low as 4 percent. Loan types include: • Homeowners: Up to $200,000 to repair or replace a primary residence • Renters or homeowners: Up to $40,000 to replace or repair personal property, like clothing, furniture, cars, or appliances • Businesses: Up to $2 million to meet financial obligations or operating expenses during the storms To qualify for funding, applicants must meet FEMA eligibility guidelines and file a claim with their insurance provider. Federal support is available only to assist with costs not already covered by insurance, or to those who do not have insurance. How to apply Applications are due by March 16 and can be done online at DisasterAssistance.gov, or by phone at 1-800-621-3362, or in person at the Alameda County Disaster Recovery Center, 7001 Oakport Street, Oakland. articles.text: Who’s ready for seconds? After a tremendous community turnout last year to Piedmont’s inaugural multicultural festival, Piedmont Food Fest returns to Piedmont Park on Sunday, April 2, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. with a curated culinary and entertainment showcase that’ll offer something for everyone. In the spirit of celebrating the diversity of the Bay Area through food, art, and music, Piedmont Food Fest encourages attendees to sample new experiences together while learning the stories behind the chefs, artists, and businesses. Visitors this year can look forward to an expanded experience with over 15 food vendors (including the crowd-pleasing birria tacos from La Santa Torta, pork belly baos from The Chairman, and dishes from the migrant chefs of James Beard Award-winning food incubator Oakland Bloom). Also included more than 10 locally renowned breweries and wineries, including Federation Brewing, Oakland United, and 2 Broads Cider. The KidZone midway will be part of the mix, and live performances will take place, such as Emeryville Taiko and Oakland Samba Revue. The Food Fest is also collaborating with Piedmont schools to feature student art contributions. The Food Fest team encourages attendees to invite friends and family to join us for a memorable day in the park. The Food Fest team will also be offering Early Bird packages in the coming weeks so join the mailing list at www.piedmontfoodfest.org for the latest updates as well as learn about opportunities to sponsor or volunteer at the event.

articles.text: A new Health class will be added to the middle school curriculum next year. To make way in the school curriculum, 7th graders will no longer have the option to take a semester of a foreign language as an elective. The changes were approved by the Piedmont School Board on February 8. The Health class will include sexual health, nutrition and eating disorders, drugs, alcohol, tobacco, and vaping, mental, emotional and social health and internet safety. “The plan is for all of Spanish 1, Mandarin 1, and French 1 to be taught in 8th grade,’ the board background document states. “Students will have the same amount of world language instruction in middle school; therefore, there is no impact on the world language program,” Mary Wells, a former president of the Piedmont Language School (PLS), called into the school board meeting to question the wisdom of the decision. “I have sat on the board of Piedmont Language School for the last 10 years, and during this time I have seen the district’s support for teaching world languages decline. Piedmont was already behind in teaching foreign languages in middle school,” Wells said. “It is well understood by language educators that there is a time and age factor in learning foreign languages. The younger the kids are, the quicker and better they will learn. Waiting until eighth grade to have your very first exposure to a foreign language is very late in the game,” stated current Language School president Jennifer Poole. The district faces difficult decisions whenever a new course is added. Due to the limit of courses available in the average school day, an existing course is removed to make space on the curriculum for a new course. The decision suggests that the district is moving away from teaching health topics by PE teachers, core teachers and science teachers. “A health course taught by a credentialed health teacher will greatly benefit our middle school students and prepare them for high school when they will be making many more decisions on their own about their health,” the district background document states. “It would be really nice for PUSD to reconsider its relationship with Piedmont Language School,” said Wells. We actually have to turn away classes because we cannot get classrooms – classrooms that we have to pay for. Other districts don’t charge their language schools just to use their classrooms,” Wells added.
articles.title: PMS to add Health class & drop 7th grade foreign language

articles.text: At the February 8 School Board meeting, the Piedmont Teachers Union (APT) and the school district agreed on points of discussion for negotiations scheduled for some time in March. While salaries were put on the backburner, certain specific items were previewed by APT President Elise Marks. Some of the items include: • In the Safety Conditions portion of their contract, APT would like in writing, a guarantee that the new MERV filter in HVAC systems will remain and be maintained. “We’ve valued the cleaner air in our classrooms, both for control of infection and for dealing with pollution from wildfires,” said Marks. • Teachers will be viewing the Hours and Professional Responsibility portion of their contract, which is to clarify the duties of each position. “As the budget tightens and our staff shrinks, people inevitably get asked to take on additional duties not in their job descriptions when they were hired,” said Marks. For example some elementary Special Ed. teachers have given the duty of administering intake screeners for students who might need Special Ed. services. articles.text: The Piedmont High School shield was designed in 1922. Piedmont is a small town with deep traditions. Here are three traditions that are over 50 years old. One of the long-standing traditions dates to the construction of the first Piedmont High School in 1921. The High School opened with an expected enrollment of 250 students. At the end of the first week, there were 360 students and 400 students by the end of the first semester. These students came from 14 secondary schools. In order to create a cohesive student body, the 1922 Clan-OLog – the year of the school’s first graduation class, tells us that the Rob Roy, as the school’s mascot, began in 1959. He appeared at each football game with the cheerleaders and pom-pom girls. This Scottish theme is still strong in many aspects of the school. The school’s athletic teams are called the Highlanders, sometimes Scots. T he 1924 Clan- O -Log describes the students’ thoughts on naming the first yearbook in 1922. “From the Scotch [sic], we have coined the word Clan-OThe Highland Lassies danced the Highland Fling during halftime at a 1961 Piedmont football game. student body officers selected the school colors and the school motto. They also designed the school shield and created the Clan-O-Log that first year. They chose purple and white as the school colors. As noted on the High School’s website, “Royal purple symbolizes regality and suggests to all Piedmont students, the necessity of learning to rule their lives and ambitions by the mastery of their own thoughts and actions. White represents purity and suggests that true PHS students will strive to be pure in thought, speech, and act.” The student body officers then chose the school’s motto, “Achieve the Honorable,” meaning that all students demonstrate academic and personal integrity in their work. Students worked together to design the school shield with classic symbols of a winged sandal (athletic ambitions), torch (scholastic achievement), the helmet of knighthood (bravery, courtesy, honor), Minerva (patron goddess of wisdom) and the open book that shows knowledge is open to those who will learn. These were intended to address all aspects of student life. Log, Clan standing for the students and Log meaning history.” The yearbook was to be a record of all the students. The Piedmont Highlander is the student newspaper. Sweatshirts and T-shirts are printed with “Highlanders.” The Highland Fling Spring Carnival dates to 1922, and the Alpha Clan honor society began in 1924. The school’s fight song was adapted from “On, Wisconsin” with Scottish references: A Scottish Theme The students also chose a Scottish theme. Piedmont is a highland, like Scotland. The Scots were never conquered, hence the Piedmont spirit to never give up. We are Piedmont’s fighting Scotsmen, Bold and bonny bunch! We eat thistles for our breakfast, Granite for our lunch, Munch, munch, munch … We are Piedmont’s fighting Scotsmen, Come from Highlands brown … So fight, Piedmont, Fight till every foe is down! In the 1960s, the Scottish Highland theme was at the High School football games. Rob Roy became the official school mascot in 1959 and was on the field during all the games. At halftime, the Kiltie Band played, and the Highland Lassies danced the Highland Fling. Today, the words to the fight song have been changed from “fighting Clansmen” to “fighting Scotsmen.” The yearbook name was changed from “Clan-O-Log” to “The Pride” in May 2018. Bird Calling Contest The Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest has been a beloved tradition since 1963 when a student approached biology teacher Leonard Waxdeck and asked, “Can we do something to liven things up around here?” Waxdeck gave the students an assignment to select a bird, give a report on that bird and give its authentic bird call. The raucous bird calls drew the attention of students in nearby classrooms who came to see what the noise was. What began as an exercise quickly outgrew his classroom and moved to the home economics classroom, a larger space. One year later it was moved to the school auditorium. The contest evolved into a highly competitive contest with elaborate skits and (sometimes) costumes. The top winners were flown to the Johnny Carson Show in Burbank, and later the Late Night Show with David Letterman in New York to perform their bird calls. This television exposure brought international attention to the Bird Calling Contest and to the community of Piedmont. Television performances ended when Letterman retired in 2015. Today, after 55 years, the Bird Calling Contest continues to fill the Alan Harvey Theater at the High School each spring. articles.text: PHS girls beat No. 14 Sacred Heart 2-0, No. 6 Sonoma Academy 4-1 Staff Photos Freshman Miranda Liu scored a hat trick against No. 6 Sonoma Academy. Piedmont’s No. 3 seeded girls’ soccer team has punched its ticket to the Division 4 North Coast Section semifinals and is set to face No. 2 Urban in San Francisco tonight, February 22. The Highlanders have looked strong this postseason, beating No. 14 Sacred Heart 2-0 in the first round on February 15 and handling No. 6 Sonoma Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals on February 18. PHS senior and UC San Diegobound forward Emily Fitzgerald continued her impressive season, scoring both goals against Sacred Heart and adding one more against Sonoma Academy. Fitzgerald, a four-year starter, has scored eight NCS goals in seven appearances, including four in the 2022 first round against College Prep. “I honestly think I play better against good competition. NCS just brings out the competitive side of everybody and the most competitive side of me,” said Fitzgerald. A multi-goal performance when the playoff lights are bright is proving to be a habit for Piedmont forwards. Freshman Miranda Liu scored a 3-goal hat trick against Sonoma Academy, two of which came in the second half to put the game away. The speedy freshman often uses her pace to stretch defenses. “My sister and parents are here and it was great to score in front of them… I feel like I’m pretty fast and that’s one of the things in my game,” said Liu. The Highlanders will now travel to No. 2 Urban in San Francisco for the NCS Semifinals tonight. With a win, they’ll face No. 1 University or No. 4 Marin Catholic for the NCS championship. 4-1 win vs. No. 6 Sonoma Academy Piedmont’s first goal came in the 19th minute after Ellie DeVan drew a corner. On the ensuing play, Cameron Lorin connected with a perfect cross to Fitzgerald on a well-timed near-post run, finishing with a first-touch shot into the bottom corner. Liu scored her first goal 10 minutes later on a well-timed run to create a 1-on-1 situation. In the buildup, Lorin sent a long ball out of the back to Liu starting her run. The ball was placed well enough to skim just over the leaping defenders’ head and then successfully corralled by Liu. Sonoma Academy got one goal back in the 35th minutes on a counterattack, making it 2-1 at the half. But in the second half, it didn’t take long for Piedmont to extend the lead with Liu’s next goal in the 45th. In the buildup, Audrey Lam sent a pass through the defense to the freshman attacker, Emily Fitzgerald scored twice against Sacred Heart and once against Sonoma Academy. She has scored eight NCS goals in seven appearances.

articles.text: Yosemite National Park is currently open for business and one of the highlights is the annual Firefall at Horsetail Falls. The “Firefall” is a natural phenomenon where the setting sun provides refracting light from Horsetail Falls to create a spectacular orange illusion. The event typically occurs between February 10 through the end of the month, requiring clear skies around sunset in order for it to be seen, It is also dependent upon sufficient amount of water flowing in Horsetail Falls. In order to manage traffic and crowds drawn to the phenomenon, Yosemite National Park is requiring reservations to enter the park for each weekend in February. Park officials are timing the release of reservations for the last two weekends of February at www.Recreation.gov. Current weather forecast shows mostly cloudy skies throughout the end of the month, meaning Firefall seekers should be paying close attention to developments in the weather. Sunday, February 19, may be the best bet, currently the only day with mostly clear forecast. Snow is expected to enter the area on February 22 and stretch into the first week of March. Those interested in lodging at Yosemite may contact www.travelyosemite.com, but availability at the Curry Village and Yosemite Valley Lodge is limited. For Curry Village, there are currently spots available for Friday, February 17, and February 19-25. articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco is currently hosting a major art exhibit, Sargent and Spain, showing the influence of Spain on Sargent’s work, The exhibit is on view through May 14 in the only West Coast show. When we encounter the paintings of John Singer Sargent (1856- 1925), we see a degree of freshness and spontaneity that would lead him to be the most celebrated portrait artist of his era. The demand for his portrait work allowed him to travel the world, with stops in Italy, France, and Spain. Each one of these locales would leave its own unique imprint on the artist. The U.S. provided an incredible commission opportunity. In Paris, Sargent’s aesthetic was greatly shaped in the studio of Emile Carolous Duran, and of course, Italy is Italy. Sargent’s time in Spain was equally impactful. His pilgrimages to the Museo del Prado inspired him with the work of the Baroque master Diego Velazquez. He was mesmerized by some of the Islamic architecture in southern Spain. Meanwhile, his experiences with the Spanish culture provided him with endless inspiration. Join art historian Michael Stehr as he celebrates the work of John Singer Sargent with an illustrated lecture designed to prepare the visitor for the exhibition. The art lecture will be on Friday, March 10, at 6:30 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Tickets are $20 at the door (cash only). articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s exhibit of the work of Bay Area figurative artist Joan Brown will remain open to the public through March 12 with 80 colorful paintings and sculptures from the celebrated artist. Brown is considered one of San Francisco’s most important local artists. She was once dismissed by critics as ‘unserious,’ but was recognized for her influential artistry after her untimely death in 1990. Works on display include The Dancers in a City #2 and Gordon, Joan and Rufus in Front of S.F. Opera House, which both show how much influence the city of San Francisco had on Brown’s art. Her work was included in SFMOMA’s annual exhibits in both 1957 and 1958. She was the youngest artist exhibited as part of Young America 1960 (Thirty American Painters Under Thirty-Six) at the Whitney Museum of American Art. “We are thrilled to present Joan Brown, a reassessment of the unabashedly personal, defiantly independent and enduringly relevant career of one of San Francisco’s most important local heroes,” said Janet Bishop, Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. Visit www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/joan-brown/ to learn more. Museum hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Fridays through Tuesdays and 1 to 8 p.m. on Thursdays. The museum is closed Wednesdays. The Joan Brown exhibit at the SF Museum of Modern Art remains on view through March 12.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s production of Giselle opens this week on Friday, February 24, at the War Memorial Opera House. Performances continue through March 5. Helgi Tomasson’s Giselle is part of the company’s 2023 Repertory Season. Costume and lighting design is by Danish artist Mikael Melbye. Set to a score by Adolphe Adams, the ballet tells the story of a young peasant girl, Giselle, who falls madly in love with nobleman Albrecht. When his true identity is revealed by his rival Hilarion, Giselle goes mad and dies of heartbreak. The two-act ballet is set in Rhineland during the Middle Ages. It is widely hailed as one of the greatest romantic ballets of all time. Giselle premiered at Paris Opera Ballet in 1841. San Francisco Ballet first presented Giselle in 1947, and it was last performed by the company in 2015. “The whole Act II is a work of art like no other – the spirituality of it,” said SF Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo. “Very rarely, as a human body made of flesh, is a performer asked to inhabit the uninhabitable.” To view showtimes and purchase tickets, visit www.sfballet. org/discover/backstage/the-storyof-giselle/. articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre’s production of The Headlands is currently being performed at the Toni Rembe Theatre in downtown San Francisco through March 5. The Headlands is Obie Award-winning playwright Christopher Chen’s newest play, described as “a complicated love letter” to San Francisco. The play tells the story of true crime fan Henry Wong, whose father’s unexplained death is the ultimate cold case. Protagonist Wong digs into the San Francisco police department evidence, but he’s haunted by the past of his own family history and upbringing. “I am thrilled beyond measure to be bringing The Headlands to A.C.T., and to be working with Pam MacKinnon to bring it to life. The Headlands is my love letter to San Francisco, the city I spent my entire life in – from birth up to right now. To share this play with my hometown – a place I feel so deeply in my bones – will be one of the most personally meaningful moments of my career,” said Chen. To purchase tickets and for more information, visit www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/the-headlands/. But it was the great American tenor Jan Peerce, who gave all of them the best advice he ever received: “Get a good education and take it from there.” That sounded like good advice, and he took it. It helped that he was conversant in five languages and was able to sing the grand operas of Wagner and Verdi, as well as numerous operettas in German and English. Concert and television appearances and teaching were also part of his résumé. He was so busy in Lyric tenor Cesare Curzi was originally from San Francisco’s North Beach. Europe that he didn’t have time to sing at the Met. Can you imagine singing 100-150 concerts a year? I got to know Cesare after he had formally “retired” and returned to California. articles.text: Judi Dench as Queen Victoria and Ali Fazal as Abdul Karim in Victoria & Abdul My first impression of Victoria & Abdul was of a film that seemed shallow, with very little going on other than the telling of a story about an English monarch who for some 50 years exercised unequivocal power as the titular head of Britain’s vast empire and her jarring relationship with an Indian man. Queen Victoria ruled supreme for over half a century, her colonial reach including India. Two men, Abdul (Ali Fazal) and Mohammed (Adzel Akhtar), are chosen to journey to England to present to her majesty a commemorative coin from her Indian subjects as part of her golden jubilee. The year is 1887. Victoria (Judi Dench) is now an elderly woman grown weary with life and feeling a sense of isolation after the death of her much loved husband, Albert, and two of her nine children. And so, the two Indians arrive and are immediately schooled by the palace staff in the proper way to approach the queen with their coin. They’re told to avoid eye contact no matter the circumstances. Abdul ignores his instructions and it is when he gazes at Victoria and she at him that there is a connection, one that is unexpected and one that surprises all in the royal household. Suddenly, the queen is rejuvenated, her interest in life renewed. She soon wishes only to bask in the company of Abdul. She wants to know all about his language, his culture and his family. And she wishes to learn Urdu. As well, Abdul is transformed from being a mere clerk in India to Victoria’s “Munshi,” meaning teacher and guide, a designation that is unsettling not only to the royal household, but most especially to her son, Bertie (Eddie Izzard), the Prince of Wales and heir to the thrown. Undaunted, Victoria perseveres. When thinking about the narrative, it gradually becomes clear that director Stephen Frears was not simply making a light comedy about the silly reactions by family and staff to the queen’s attachment to this strange man who is, from the point of view of her family, now fastened to the royal ship of state like a barnacle. But there is something more in play in this film. The film is actually a character study of a woman who is not only profoundly lonely, but also free of the entrenched, colonial attitudes of all those who comprise the royal household, to include England’s Prime Minister, Lord Salisbury (Michael Gabon). As a group, led by Bertie, they rebel, their hostility toward both Abdul and Mohammed palpable. They make no effort to know the two men; rather, they reject both outright based on prejudices rooted in the colonial posture of the Brits throughout their empire. Generally, their subjects, so to speak, were brown and were judged as inferior solely because of the color of their skin. Victoria harbored no such assumptions and saw in Abdul another individual who, while different in background and customs and color, was at the very least her equal. When Bertie confronts his mother, he insists that Abdul is nothing more than an opportunist. The queen, taking offense, responds, asking, “How is that any different from the rest of you?” Bertie and household are blind to their own prejudices, hence this becomes a film about racism, a wounding response to a man who could have enriched all of their lives but is instead viewed as a poseur, someone to be discarded. What Frears has done is create a movie that is disguised as a quirky, situational comedy but that is so much more. While the film is a wonderful vehicle for the talent of Judi Dench, who in every way inhabits Victoria, it also asks the audience to look just a bit further for the deeper intent of Frears. Victoria & Abdul. Directed by Stephen Frears, Starring Judi Dench, Michael Gabon, Ali Fazal. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG-13. Streaming on Prime/VUDU/Netflix/Apple tv.

articles.text: Till opens in Chicago, the year is 1955, and we’re introduced to cheeky 14-year-old Emmett Till (Jaylyn Hall) who is preparing to spend the summer visiting his cousins and his uncle Moses (John Douglas Thompson) for the first time, Moses is a sharecropper and they live in the deep South in the town of Money, Mississippi. Having never been out of Chicago, he is encouraged to make the trip by his grandmother, Alma (Whoopie Goldberg), who thinks it’s time he met his extended family. His single mother, Mamie (Danielle Deadwyler), is not so sure and she tells Emmett that when it comes to being among white people the rules for black people are different and he must “make himself small.” He hears the words but doesn’t understand the message. For reasons unexplained Mamie doesn’t sit her much loved son down and conveys to him the seriousness of what she is saying. Mississippi is not Chicago in ways that Emmett cannot begin to comprehend. It is a state where the Ku Klux Klan is active and part of the culture. And so, Emmett boards the train and for the last time waves goodbye to his mother and grandmother, having no idea, in all his innocence, where he is headed. He will be a stranger in a strange land. It is impossible not to anticipate with a sense of dread what awaits him. On a sunny afternoon his cousins and uncle stop at a mercantile store. Emmett goes inside to buy some candy and without thinking is overly friendly with the cashier, a white woman, Carolyn Bryant (Haley Bennett). Taken by her good looks, he whistles at her as his cousins look on in horror for they, unlike Emmett, realize what he has done, and in that moment the white supremacy of the South, that become evident. Emmett is kidnapped, tortured, and lynched. This is done with a sense of impunity that is unimaginable. His body is found later, floating in the Talahatchie River, beaten and bloated. When Mamie and Alma learn that Emmett has been killed their grief is beyond comprehension, mixed with disbelief and a consuming rage. When she finally manages to get Emmett’s barely recognizable body returned to her she makes a fateful, shocking decision that his funeral casket will be open so all who pass by will be forced to view his unreconstructed remains. His horrible visage will soon become a Black media sensation. When two men are charged (the brother-in-law and husband of Carolyn) with Emmett’s murder, Mamie, against all advice, journeys to Money where she takes the witness stand and gives dramatic testimony to an allwhite male jury. When asked if she is going to stay in town to await the verdict, Mamie bitterly says no, she knows what the outcome will be. And so it is, the men are found not guilty. The performance by Danielle Deadwyler as the grief-stricken mother is Oscar-worthy and yet she was inexplicably passed over. Hopefully, Till will join what has become a pantheon of extraordinary films that touch on America’s history of racism. Till. Directed by Chinonye Chukwu. Starring Danielle Deadwyler, Jaylyn Hall, and Whoopie Goldberg. 2 hrs., 10 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2022. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Evangeline Lilly and Paul Rudd in Ant-Man and the Wasp Ant-Man (2015) was an unexpected hit and soon joined what is now referred to as the Marvel Cinematic Universe, a galaxy of superhero characters. If you’re a kid, you didn’t have to suspend your disbelief even for a moment, no matter how outlandish the premise for the original Ant-Man movie was. It starred Scott Lang (Paul Rudd) and his mentor, Dr. Hank Pym (Michael Douglas), who design a special suit allowing Scott to shrink himself at will while mind-melding with ants. Having demonstrated its audience chops, meaning the unequivocal appeal to the tween/ teen crowd, a sequel was inevitable, hence Ant-Man and the Wasp. Same crew plus some extras. Only now, Hank’s daughter, Hope (Angeline Lilly), aka the Wasp, takes stage center and demonstrates real athleticism buzzing about, wearing her own designer suit – plus a serious arsenal of stun gun weapons. Using Hank’s device, she, like Scott, can go small and then full-size, as can their cars and buildings. The plot of Wasp is simple. Hank and Hope have picked up a vibe, along with Scott, that Janet (Michelle Pfeiffer), Hank’s wife and Hope’s mom, who 30 years ago vanished into the Quantum Realm (reduction on steroids) is still alive. Their plan is to design an intricate tunnel with craft that will allow them to find her and bring her back. Getting in the way is a black market villain, Sonny Burch (Walton Groggin), and his crew of wide shouldered baddies, who want to steal Hank’s lab (reduced to the size of carry-on luggage with a handle) that’s filled with the good stuff. Act two: chase scenes, slowed down with some barely relevant exposition, go miniaturize, then back to normal, and even reach the height of 50 feet. Lots of action. Rinse and repeat. Of course, the skinny plot embellishments barely make any sense. But logical coherence is not required. There’s even a character called Ghost/Ava (Hannah John-Kamen) who appears and fades, then reappears. articles.text: Walking through town, it becomes clear to me that two things stand out as chief characteristics of the architecture in Piedmont. The first is the individuality of the homes — virtually all of the homes are “one-off” designs, built before the advent of seemingly ubiquitous tract homes. Today, even in many expensive new communities, because of economy of scale, developers often build the same home in large groups, robbing the place of the rich character, individuality and texture of the streets and community that we see here. The second observation is the high quality of design and construction throughout the city. Part of the pre-tract home era in which Piedmont was started, also included noted individual architects for each house. We benefited from (and continue to benefit from) the talents and expertise of an era of excellent local architects, including Julia Morgan, Albert Farr, Miller Warneke, and W.H. Weeks. This valuable contribution continues today with top designers and architects such as Mark Becker, Glen Jarvis, and John Malick to name just a few. And with top designers seems to come a higher level of craftsmanship which results in buildings that not only look better, but last for generations. What most people immediately think of when reference is made to architecture, is the exterior appearance of a building. As we will see in this series, although the exterior shape, form or style is only part of what can be considered good architecture, it is of course very important. It is important not only for the owners, but also for the many people experiencing it: guests, neighbors and passers-by. A building and its visual relationship to adjoining buildings and landscapes (its context) necessarily is a part of and helps form the entire community. This is why building height, massing, and lot coverage are so important and written into our zoning codes and design review requirements. There are many other visual considerations that architects work with: the entry, and entry experience; the “fenestration” or window and door sizes, shapes and locations; the materials, the textures of walls, roofs and details, the colors, the relationship to exterior landscape features, not to mention the functional program requirements of the users. How all these elements are proportioned, how they are arranged together, make up the architectural character. Regardless of the style, size, or type of building, successful architectural design needs to form a coherent whole with all parts and pieces of the design in the same family, integrated, to create a visually attractive look and impression. The feeling we get from a building is really what’s important. Often we are able to see and experience a building and like it or not like it, even if we are unable to articulate why. We will be exploring these different elements in future columns. I continue to encourage everyone to walk around, look, reflect, and form opinions of the different principles being discussed. articles.text: The Notre Dame Cathedral, known to hundreds of millions of people worldwide prior to the 2019 fire, was built in the 13th century on the Ile de La Cite, one of the two natural islands on the Seine at the center of Paris. Construction began in 1163 under the tutelage of one of France’s most imminent national heroes, Bishop of Paris Maurice de Sully who is credited with creating a Gothic architectural monument that stunned the medieval world and is universally known and loved. The French king thoroughly approved Sully’s plan for Paris having the grandest cathedral in Europe. Conceived at a height of 107-foot, none was taller; and Sully’s master builders executed methods not yet reliably tested, such as ribbed vault supports and massive flying buttresses. (Saint Denis Basilica with its flying buttresses was constructed about the same time.) The earlier known site for Notre-Dame “to our lady” was built in the late 6th century by the Franks kingdom embracing Christianity. It was destroyed by Vikings in the mid-9th century; and again rebuilt. By the 12th century with Europe in a time of peace and a growing Paris population, the French king and powerful Bishop Sully began to build a Notre Dame cathedral for the ages. articles.text: Much loved longtime Piedmont resident Lois Scott Westmont passed away on December 15, 2022, at the age of 91. She had very fond memories of her childhood in Butte, Montana with brothers Don and Owen and parents Clella and Jesse L. Scott. Lois called Piedmont home for over 50 years. Lois is survived by her three children, Karen, Jeff and Clark, and four grandchildren: Taylor, Jessica, Joshua and Zachary. She is also survived by her brother, Don Scott. Lois will be remembered for her kindness, intelligence, her love of elegance, and her quiet stoicism. According to Monsignor Chauvet commenting in December, “there’s a 50% chance the structure might not be saved.” Security guards first heard the fire alarm at 6:20 p.m. and evacuated the cathedral of visitors despite not detecting a fire. A probable unofficial report is that the guard checked the incorrect attic. As early as 6:30 pm smoke was visibly pouring from the roof. At 6:40 pm the alarm sounded again, and this time the guards called in the fire. Firefighters arrived at 6:50 p.m. Invariably, fire officials are being criticized for a response too slow. Early scrutiny of the fire’s origin fell on the firms working to rebuild the spire in a $6.8 million renovation centered in the attic that ignited the roof. One, a major scaffolding company, and the other a specialty firm for art conservancy, provided employees for police questioning. Both firms immediately denied responsibility stating that their workers had left an hour before the fire broke out. Authorities still haven’t yet announced the cause of the fire, although an electrical short circuit is widely considered as the likely cause during the renovation in the attic. It’s rumored that investigators are not admitted to the site due to safety risks. Historical decisions about the cathedral’s severe lack of fire safeguards, like firewalls and sprinkler systems, is viewed as a contributing factor. The Notre Dame cathedral is a developing story.
